list.listitem: Women should be evaluated for a cause of amenorrhea if they have not started menarche by the age of 15 years. C
Women with a history of regular menses should be evaluated for a cause of amenorrhea if they have missed 3 cycles. C

Evaluation of primary amenorrhea is generally directed by the presence or absence of secondary sexual characteristics and should include follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), leuteinizing hormone (LH), and karyotype analysis if no uterus is present or FSH and LH levels are elevated. In women with secondary sexual characteristics, evaluation for an intact vagina and uterus should be done. C
Evaluation of secondary amenorrhea should include ruling out pregnancy; if negative for pregnancy, the workup begins with FSH, LH, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin. C

background.definition: Primary amenorrhea is the absence of menarche by age 15 years when normal secondary sexual characteristics are present or within 3 years of thelarche (breast budding). Failure to develop secondary sexual characteristics by age 13 years also necessitates investigation. Secondary amenorrhea is the absence of menses for 3 months in women with previously normal menstruation or the absence of menses for 9 months in women with previous oligomenorrhea (i.e., a menstrual interval of >35 days or a decrease in the number of bleeding episodes). In order to avoid overdiagnosis of amenorrhea in adolescents, there has been a recommendation that irregular menstrual cycles represent normal pubertal transition in adolescents <1 year post menarche .

list.listitem: Among female breast cancer patients who receive adjuvant chemotherapy, chemotherapy-induced amenorrhea occurs in about half (55%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 50%-60%).
The prevalence of amenorrhea not due to pregnancy or menopause is about 3%.

Authors of a systematic review including 8 studies found psychological factors associated with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea including higher levels of anxiety, sleep disorders, depression and eating attitudes, especially drive for thinness.
See for causes of primary and secondary amenorrhea.

In a genetic study of women with primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), which is cessation of menses before age 40 years, eight significant copy number variations and five candidate genes were identified. This condition is also associated with a permutation in the FMR1 gene for Fragile X.
Susceptibility genes are also being examined in women with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (a reversible form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone [GnRH] deficiency commonly triggered by stressors).
Investigators using whole exome sequencing in 4 Iranian families found diverse genetic causes of amenorrhea even within the same family.

In a study including 381 women with the history of amenorrhea, most (77%) had a normal karyotype (46, XX). Of those with abnormal karyotypes, the majority (61%) had abnormalities of X chromosome, followed by 27.2% with Y chromosome abnormalities and 11.8% with rearrangements between autosomal and/or sex chromosomes.
In addition to chromosomal abnormalities, POI can be caused by radiation or chemotherapy and xenobiotic agents (e.g., chemicals, pharmaceuticals) which can accelerate ovarian reserve depletion.

POI can also be of autoimmune origin, characterized by serum ovarian, adrenocortical, or steroidogenic cell autoantibodies. There is a published case series of three women with autoimmune POI triggered by receipt of the human papilloma virus vaccine.
Although rare, androgen insensitivity syndrome can cause amenorrhea in a phenotypic female who is genetically male.
Amenorrhea has many causes but results from a failure in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis to produce the cyclic changes of the endometrium required to cause menses.

Authors of a systematic review of exercise-induced oligomenorrhea concluded that hyperandrogenism, similar to that observed in polycystic ovary syndrome, may be causal for some women versus hypothalamic inhibition due to an energy deficiency.

Differential.Differential_Features: Dysmorphic features: webbed neck, short stature, widely spaced nipples
Anosmia (absence of the sense of smell)
Breast development, but minimal or no pubic hair presence
Normal secondary sexual characteristics, but absent or rudimentary vagina and/or uterus
Buffalo hump, central obesity, easy bruising, hypertension, striae, proximal muscle weakness

list.listitem: History should include eliciting for weight loss, exercise habits, chronic illness, central nervous system or pelvic radiation or chemotherapy, menarche and previous menstrual history, sexual activity, and psychosocial stressors.

Additional history items suggested by the Endocrine Society for evaluation of patients with suspected functional amenorrhea include diet and eating disorders, attitudes such as perfectionism and high need for social approval, ambitions and expectations for self and others, sleep patterns, mood and fractures.

Ask about illicit, prescription, and nonprescription drug use, particularly looking for use of hormonal medications, antipsychotics, antidepressants, antihypertensives, histamine receptor blockers, opiates, and cocaine.
Family history should be evaluated for genetic defects, infertility, menstrual and menopausal history of female relatives, and endocrinopathies.

Review of systems should include evaluating for symptoms of thyroid disease, galactorrhea, headache and visual disturbance, hirsutism or acne, vasomotor symptoms, anosmia, breast changes, and cyclic abdominal pain.

Physical examination should include body mass index and growth chart (when applicable), evaluation for dysmorphic features such as webbed neck, short stature, widely spaced nipples, presence of striae, central obesity, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, and thyroid examination. The examination should include evaluation of Tanner staging and pubic hair distribution.
The gynecologic examination should include an evaluation of the external genitalia, presence of clitoral hypertrophy, imperforate hymen, vaginal septum, and presence or absence of a uterus.

In a clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics, evaluation of amenorrhea in the adolescent is an indication for a pelvic examination; authors recommend prior education, patient control of the process, and use of relaxation techniques and a Huffman or smaller size disposable speculum (shorter width).

Evaluation of primary amenorrhea is generally directed by the presence or absence of secondary sexual characteristics; appropriate laboratory testing may include FSH, LH, and karyotype analysis. Additional testing options include a pregnancy test, progestin challenge test and ultrasound looking for anatomic abnormalities.
Evaluation of primary amenorrhea in women with normal secondary sexual characteristics should include imaging with ultrasound for the presence of a normal uterus.
Evaluation of secondary amenorrhea should include a pregnancy test.
Appropriate laboratory evaluation of secondary amenorrhea, once pregnancy is excluded, includes thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), prolactin, FSH, and LH.

The Endocrine Society (2017) also recommends obtaining estradiol and anti-Müllerian hormone to complete the endocrine workup for women with suspected functional amenorrhea. In addition, they recommend obtaining a beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose, bicarbonate, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, liver panel, and (when appropriate) sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein levels.

In women with POI, as evidenced by high levels of FSH and LH and low estradiol, laboratory tests should include 17-hydroxyprogesterone (if high level, consider congenital adrenal hyperplasia), cortisol (if high level, consider Cushing; if normal, consider PCOS), and testosterone levels (if moderately high, consider PCOS; if very high, consider malignancy). If FSH is normal or low, order estradiol; if low, consider hypothalamic amenorrhea or pituitary dysfunction (e.g., Sheehan’s syndrome, stress or exercise-induced, or anorexia).

In women with secondary amenorrhea, a progestogen challenge test can determine whether adequate estrogenization is present for menstruation, and an estrogen-progestogen test can differentiate inadequate estrogenization from an outflow tract obstruction. Certain tests, listed below, may help predict the patient's response to the progestogen challenge test.

In specific cases of secondary amenorrhea, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is indicated to evaluate for prolactinoma or pituitary tumor. This should be suspected in women with headaches; persistent non-self-induced vomiting; visual changes, thirst, or urination not attributable to other causes; lateralizing neurologic signs; or clinical signs and/or laboratory results that suggest pituitary hormone deficiency or excess. In women with hyperprolactinemia, pituitary tumors are responsible for almost 50% of cases; galactorrhea occurs in less than 50% of these patients.

The Endocrine Society also recommends assessing bone density via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) for any adolescent or woman with six or more months of amenorrhea, and earlier in patients with a history or suspicion of severe nutritional deficiency, other energy deficit states, and/or skeletal fragility.
See for a detailed list of causes of amenorrhea.
Inpatient evaluation should be considered for patients with functional amenorrhea and severe bradycardia, hypotension, orthostasis, and/or electrolyte imbalance.

See algorithms for primary () and secondary () amenorrhea. The Endocrine Society also suggests a diagnostic evaluation for functional amenorrhea in adolescents and women whose menstrual cycle interval persistently exceeds 45 days.
See for drug dosages used in estrogen/progesterone challenge tests.
